name: Grünfeld Defense, Three Knights
summary: The Three Knights Grünfeld (D90) meets 3...d5 with 4.Nf3 Bg7, keeping flexible Bf4, Bg5 or Qb3 setups while Black pressures d4 along the long diagonal.
intro: The Three Knights Variation is a flexible Grünfeld move order that appears after 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Nf3 Bg7. Rather than resolving the central tension at once with the Exchange 4.cxd5, White develops the king's knight and keeps every option open. The name marks the three minor pieces already in play, and from here White can steer toward the Russian System with Qb3, quiet lines with Bf4 or Bg5, a restrained setup with e3, or simply transpose back into main-line Grünfeld theory. Black, meanwhile, pursues the classic Grünfeld idea: allow White a broad pawn centre, fianchetto the dark-squared bishop, and then chip away at d4 with pieces and the ...c5 break. The result is a rich, dynamic struggle between a mobile centre and energetic counterattack.
line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 d5 Nf3 Bg7

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: As in every Grünfeld, the fight is about White's centre. Black willingly concedes central space, trusting that the bishop on g7, pressure down the long diagonal, and the levers ...c5 and sometimes ...e5 will turn White's broad pawn front into a liability rather than a strength. By choosing 4.Nf3 instead of the immediate Exchange, White declines to build the classic c3-and-e4 pawn duo straight away, keeping the structure fluid and inviting a more positional, manoeuvring game.

White's flexibility is the whole point. Depending on Black's reaction, White can pressure d5 with Qb3, complete development with Bf4 or Bg5 and e3, or hold back the centre, always retaining the option to transpose into a favourable version of a known line. Black must therefore be ready for several structures, meeting each with the same underlying recipe of piece pressure on the centre, quick castling, and timely pawn breaks that keep White's pawns from becoming a strong, mobile mass.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: After 4...Bg7 White's most testing continuation is 5.Qb3, the Russian System move order, when 5...dxc4 6.Qxc4 O-O reaches a well-known main line in which White enjoys a mobile centre and Black targets it with ...a6, ...b5, ...Bg4 and ...Nc6 or ...Nbd7. Quieter is 5.Bf4, developing before committing the centre, met by 5...O-O 6.Rc1 or the sharp 5...dxc4. The pin 5.Bg5 invites 5...Ne4, striking at the pinning bishop with immediate piece play.

White can also keep things solid with 5.e3, when Black castles and prepares ...c5, or transpose directly with 5.cxd5 Nxd5 6.e4 into the Exchange Grünfeld. In each case Black relies on the same plan: fianchetto, castle, and pressure d4 with ...c5, ...Nc6 and the g7-bishop. Because White has kept the position flexible, precise move orders matter, and both sides angle to reach the structure they know best while avoiding the opponent's preparation.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The Grünfeld Defence, in which Black allows a big centre only to bombard it, was pioneered by the Austrian grandmaster Ernst Grünfeld in the 1920s and became a mainstay of dynamic, counterattacking chess. The 4.Nf3 move order, developing three minor pieces before clarifying the centre, has long appealed to players who prefer flexibility to early commitment.

It is a common route into the Russian System and other main lines and remains a frequent guest at the top level, where subtle move-order finesses are prized. By delaying cxd5, White keeps Black guessing about the eventual structure and can often reach a preferred setup, which is why the Three Knights remains a practical and theoretically respected way to handle the Grünfeld.

keyIdeas: White develops 4.Nf3 before clarifying the centre, keeping options open.
The move order can transpose to Russian System, Bf4, Bg5 or Exchange lines.
Black allows a broad centre and attacks it with the g7-bishop and ...c5.
Qb3 pressures d5 and eyes recapturing on c4 after ...dxc4.
Piece pressure and the ...c5 lever are Black's constant counterplay.
Flexibility lets White steer toward a favourable known structure.

white: Develop with Nf3, keeping the central tension unresolved.
Pressure d5 with Qb3, entering Russian System channels.
Complete development with Bf4 or Bg5 and e3 before committing.
Retain the option to transpose into the Exchange Grünfeld.
Build and defend a mobile centre that cramps Black.
black: Strike at White's centre with the ...c5 break.
Meet Qb3 with ...dxc4 and queenside expansion by ...a6 and ...b5.
Keep the long diagonal open for the g7-bishop's pressure.
